question: What is the average-case time complexity of HashMap.get() and HashMap.put()?
explanation: HashMap is a hash table, so get and put are O(1) on average. Worst case is O(log n) per bucket in modern Java, since heavily-collided buckets become red-black trees.

question: You need to build a long string by appending inside a loop. Which approach is preferred, and why?
choices: StringBuilder, because String is immutable and += copies on every iteration
String +=, because the compiler always optimizes it into one buffer
String.concat(), because it mutates the string in place
char[] only, because StringBuilder is deprecated
explanation: Java Strings are immutable; += in a loop creates a new String (and copies the accumulated content) on each iteration, which is O(n^2) overall. StringBuilder appends into a growable buffer in amortized O(1) per append.

question: Which statement about ArrayList and LinkedList index access is true?
choices: ArrayList.get(i) is O(1); LinkedList.get(i) is O(n)
ArrayList.get(i) is O(n); LinkedList.get(i) is O(1)
explanation: ArrayList is backed by an array, so index access is constant time. LinkedList must walk node-by-node from the nearest end, which is linear time.

question: Which Map implementation keeps its keys in sorted order, and at what cost per get/put?
explanation: TreeMap is a red-black tree: keys stay sorted and operations are O(log n). LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order (not sorted order), and HashMap has no ordering at all.
